passage: Monday. Shreya's shoulders crept up toward her ears as the audit deadline came closer, and Nazia, sitting opposite, thought she looked irritated. She avoided asking anything. Wednesday. Shreya's neck ached and she snapped at a small question about file names. Nazia went quiet and wondered what she had done wrong. Friday. Shreya caught her shoulders in the window reflection, hunched and hard, and thought, that looks angry, but I am just stretched thin. She stood, rolled her shoulders back, and walked to the balcony for five minutes. Back at her desk she told Nazia, "Sorry about Wednesday. It was the deadline, not you." Nazia laughed with relief. 🙂

qa.q: What did Shreya see in the window reflection on Friday?
qa.a: She saw her shoulders hunched and hard.

qa.q: What did Nazia first think Shreya's raised shoulders meant, and what did they turn out to mean?
qa.a: Nazia thought Shreya looked irritated, but the tension came from the audit deadline and strain. Shreya was stretched thin, not angry with Nazia.

qa.q: What small step helped Shreya on Friday?
qa.a: She rolled her shoulders back and walked to the balcony for a short break, then explained her earlier snap.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel between Monday and Friday about Shreya's behaviour?
qa.a: She felt unsure and worried she had done something wrong, which is why she went quiet and later laughed with relief.

grounding: Illustrates shoulder tension during deadlines that colleagues read as irritation when it is strain, eased by a stretch and a short break.

passage: Let me tell you about my first year as a designer, Damini. I am Tanvir, and I did the classic thing: I held my shoulders up around my ears for months. At every deadline my whole upper body turned to stone. A senior colleague, my Nani's old neighbour's son actually, watched me once and said, "You look like you are carrying a tank." I laughed but it stuck. My colleagues thought I was annoyed with them, which I never was. I began setting a small reminder on my phone: stand, roll the shoulders, look out the window. Two minutes. It did not shrink the deadline. But my neck stopped aching and people stopped tiptoeing around me. Tell your team the tension is strain, not attitude.

qa.q: What did the senior colleague say Tanvir looked like?
qa.a: The senior colleague said Tanvir looked like carrying a tank.

qa.q: What did Tanvir's colleagues believe the tight shoulders meant, and what was the truth?
qa.a: They believed Tanvir was annoyed with them, but Tanvir says that was never so and the tension came from deadlines. This shows body tension can be misread as attitude.

qa.q: What routine helped Tanvir with the strain?
qa.a: Tanvir set a phone reminder to stand, roll the shoulders and look out the window for two minutes.

qa.q: How might Damini's team have felt around Tanvir during Tanvir's first year?
qa.a: They probably felt careful and slightly nervous, as Tanvir says people tiptoed around, and they may have relaxed once the shoulders did.

grounding: Illustrates an adult holding tension in the shoulders during deadlines, read as irritation by colleagues and eased by stretching breaks.

passage: The clinic had run out of the standard forms again, and Samir, the front-desk assistant, faced a queue of patients. When Francis, an old patient, asked why nothing was ready, Samir lifted his shoulders and turned his palms up. "I know," he said, "I am sorry." Francis's face stayed tight. Samir realised the shrug alone said nothing about what he would do. So he added, "The forms are missing because I forgot to reorder them. I will write your details on a sheet now, and I will place the order today." Francis's shoulders eased. "Thank you for saying so," he said. Samir wrote quickly. 🙂

qa.q: Why was the clinic queue delayed?
qa.a: The clinic had run out of the standard forms.

qa.q: What was Francis probably feeling when Samir only shrugged, and what changed it?
qa.a: He could have taken it as helplessness or as dodging blame, which fits his tight face. Once Samir named his own mistake and a fix, Francis relaxed.

qa.q: What could Samir do in future to avoid shrugs that feel dismissive?
qa.a: He could pair a shrug with words that own the problem and say what he will do next, as he did with the sheet and the order.

qa.q: How might Francis have felt when Samir only shrugged?
qa.a: He probably felt brushed off, since the shrug did not tell him whether anyone would fix the delay.

grounding: Illustrates an adult's palms-up shrug that can feel dismissive unless words add ownership.

passage:
Dear Yogesh,

Thank you for your patience about the missing slides in Tuesday's review. In the meeting I shrugged and said, "What can I do," and I saw your face fall. I want to fix that. The truth is I sent the slides to the wrong folder, and I did not check. It was my mistake, not the printer's, not the network's. I have re-sent them and set myself a reminder to check attachments twice before sending. If you have moments during the week I would be glad to walk you through the changes. I am truly sorry for the trouble. 🙏

Yours,
Swati

qa.a: Yogesh might have felt let down or dismissed, since "What can I do" with a shrug can sound like nobody is fixing the problem.

grounding: Illustrates a shrug meant as apology or helplessness that risks feeling dismissive, followed by words that show ownership.

subtype: Hands behind the back in respect [Expressing]
passage: I work two desks from Yusuf, so I saw the whole thing. When the regional head walked into our Pune office, Yusuf stopped mid-sentence and stood with his hands clasped behind his back, chin level, listening. I am Reena, and I thought it looked very formal, almost stiff. The regional head asked him about the delivery figures and Yusuf answered clearly, still standing that way. Later in the canteen, Yusuf stood with his hands in his pockets like anyone else, joking with the driver. I cannot tell whether the earlier pose came from respect or nerves. He told me he grew up standing like that before elders at school assemblies.

qa.a: The regional head probably saw it as respectful and attentive, though a person from a more casual office could find it stiff.

subtype: Hands behind the back in respect [Expressing]
passage:

The wide arms felt inviting, but I noticed the listening mattered more than the pose.

passage:
Week 1. Jeevan, newly leading the sales group, spread his arms wide in the first meeting and said, "My door is open." People smiled, but nobody spoke. He talked for the whole hour.

Week 3. He tried it again, arms open, and this time added, "Rashmi, you have handled this client. What would you do?" She hesitated, then explained a problem in the pricing sheet. Jeevan took notes and did not interrupt.

Week 6. In the review Jeevan opened his arms and stayed quiet. Two juniors raised concerns, and Rashmi later thanked him for hearing them out. "You were listening this time," she said.

qa.q: What did Jeevan say in the first meeting?
qa.a: He said, "My door is open."

qa.q: Why did nobody speak in week 1, even though Jeevan's arms were open?
qa.a: He talked for the whole hour, so the open arms did not match his behaviour and gave people no room. The wide gesture could have been seen as welcoming, but he did not listen.

qa.q: What changed in Jeevan's approach that made people speak?
qa.a: He asked a direct question, stayed quiet and took notes without interrupting, which made the gesture real.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt in week 1 compared with week 6?
qa.a: In week 1 she might have felt unsure that speaking was welcome, while by week 6 she trusted that he would hear her out.

grounding: Illustrates a young leader spreading the arms wide to invite the team, with real effect depending on genuine listening.

Farhan

subtype: Wringing hands and grief or anxiety [Interpreting]
passage: Outside the district hospital in the small town, Rekha sat on a bench with a paper cup of tea going cold in her hands. Her sister Charu had been taken in for tests an hour ago. Rekha kept wringing her fingers, then pressing them together, then wringing again. A woman from the tea stall, who sat nearby, saw it and said nothing for a while. Then she handed Rekha a folded steel cup of water and sat beside her. "You want me to call your husband?" she asked gently. Rekha nodded. "Please," she said, and her hands finally rested on her knees.

passage: Shalini's first day at the bank branch had one small worry: how to greet people. Kavitha, her manager, extended a hand, so Shalini shook it. Then the customer coming in behind her, an older man in a white cap, held his hand to his chest and nodded. Shalini paused, then did the same. Later a colleague pressed his palms together, and she echoed that too. "How do you decide?" she asked Kavitha at lunch. "I watch what they do first," Kavitha said. "And if I am not sure I ask, 'How would you like to greet?'" Shalini wrote it down. Choosing well meant noticing the person, not a rule. 😊

qa.q: Who extended a hand to Shalini first?
qa.a: Kavitha, her manager, extended a hand.

qa.q: Why did Shalini change her greeting for each person?

qa.q: What could Shalini say if she is unsure how to greet someone?
qa.a: She could ask, "How would you like to greet?", as Kavitha does.

qa.q: How might the older man in the white cap have felt when Shalini nodded back?
qa.a: He probably felt respected and comfortable, since she met his preference instead of forcing a handshake.

passage: Deepika arrived early to the client meeting in Mumbai, with a full folder and no time to spare because the lift was out of order and her train had run late. At the door the client's team stood in a line. Deepika's hand moved toward a handshake, then she saw Farida, the client's lead, hold her hands together with a small smile. Deepika folded her own palms and said, "Namaste, I am Deepika." Farida's smile widened. A man at the end offered a handshake, and Deepika took it warmly without fuss. She made a note to herself: watch first, then match. Everyone sat down, and nobody had noticed her flustered morning.

qa.a: It showed she was paying attention to Farida's preference and wanted to be respectful, despite being flustered. Her started handshake shows how automatic the habit was.

qa.q: What could Deepika do if she is unsure how a client wants to greet?

qa.a: Farida probably felt respected, since her smile widened when Deepika met her folded-hands greeting.

passage: In the hospital lobby, Asif, a physiotherapist, watched a patient's son press his hand to his chest and say, "Thank you for everything." Asif nodded but did not quite feel it, because the man's voice was flat and his eyes were on the door. He said, "You are welcome," and moved on. Two days later, another patient, tired and smiling, put her hand over her heart, met Asif's eyes and said quietly, "You gave me my walk back. Thank you." That one landed. Karthik, the ward attendant, saw it too and said, "Same gesture, different weight." Asif thought the manner mattered more than the hand.

qa.q: What is Asif's job?
qa.a: Asif is a physiotherapist.

qa.q: Why did the second patient's gesture land differently for Asif?
qa.a: She held her hand over her heart, made eye contact and spoke quietly and specifically. The first man's flat voice and wandering eyes made the same gesture feel hurried, though he may simply have been anxious.

qa.q: What can Asif take from these two thank-yous?
qa.a: He can notice that warmth comes from the whole manner, not one gesture, and avoid judging the first man too harshly.

qa.q: How might the first patient's son have felt during that moment?
qa.a: He may have been distracted or worried, so his thank-you could have been sincere even though it did not look warm.

grounding: Illustrates a hand over the heart as thanks or sincerity, whose warmth depends on the whole manner.

passage:

When you handed me the finished report on Friday, I put my hand over my heart and said thank you, and I hope it did not look like a show. I meant it. Lokesh

subtype: Finger to lips and safety limits [Mismatch]
passage:
Dear Jyoti,

At the hospital yesterday, a nurse put a finger to her lips near the ward door and I stepped back quietly. I understood: patients were asleep. Then I thought of something else and it has been on my mind. At the cousins' wedding last month, a man I barely know put his finger to his lips and smiled when he said something about a photo he wanted me to keep between us. It was not the same. It felt like a secret I did not agree to. I decided not to keep it, and I told my aunt. She said I did the right thing. I am glad I told someone.

Ankita

qa.q: Where was the nurse when she put a finger to her lips?
qa.a: She was near the ward door at the hospital.

qa.q: Why did Ankita feel uneasy about the man at the wedding but not the nurse?
qa.a: The nurse was asking for quiet to protect sleeping patients, while the man wanted a secret she had not agreed to keep. Ankita felt the difference in what the gesture was asking for.

qa.q: What did Ankita do that was wise?
qa.a: She decided not to keep the secret and told her aunt, a trusted person.

qa.q: How might the nurse have seen the same gesture?
qa.a: The nurse used it as a polite, ordinary request for quiet, with no secret in it.

grounding: Illustrates finger-to-lips read as a polite request for quiet versus a demand for secrecy, where sharing an uncomfortable secret with a trusted person is right.

subtype: Finger to lips and safety limits [Mismatch]
passage: Fine, Naveen, here is what I have learned about the finger to the lips. Farhan speaking. In hospital corridors it is a polite request: quiet, please, patients are resting. passage: Rafiq, senior partner, told Vinita this story over tea. "When I was your age I ran weekly meetings, and one man always spoke first and longest.
